name: Straight-front corset

card.summary: An 1890s corset designed by Inès Gaches-Sarraute with a long straight busk that supports the abdomen and, through exaggeration, produced the upright, forward-tilted S-curve silhouette of c. 1900.
card.aka: Health corset; abdominal corset; swan-bill corset; S-bend corset; Gaches-Sarraute corset
card.note: Historical garment; a 1910 physician's study and modern reenactor tests describe breathing and comfort limits.

quick.overview:
The straight-front corset is a corset introduced in the 1890s by the French physician Inès Gaches-Sarraute. She designed it as a medical garment, with a straight, flat busk that supported and lifted the abdomen rather than squeezing the waist, to ease gynaecological problems patients blamed on older corsets.

Its appearance payoff was the fashionable Edwardian silhouette of about 1900 to 1908: a flattened front, low bust, arched back and a posture tilted forward from the hips. Historians note that fashion exaggerated her design into the S-curve shape, and tests by a 1910 physician and by modern reenactors report that it still limited breathing.
quick.how: In period practice the corset was worn under dresses, with shape coming largely from the cut of the fabric and flexible boning, and wearers adopted a particular poised stance to complete the silhouette. Today it appears mainly in costume, reenactment and historical-dress circles.
quick.risks: Physician Robert Latou Dickinson, studying the S-line corset in 1910, concluded it still limited diaphragmatic breathing and pushed downward on the pelvis. A treadmill test with reenactors found higher breathing and heart rates after exercise in a 1900s straight-front corset.

lead: The straight-front corset is a style of corset introduced in the 1890s by the French physician and corsetière Inès Gaches-Sarraute (1853-1928). She developed what she called a health or abdominal corset because she was concerned about gynaecological problems that her patients attributed to corsets, and set out her design in the 1900 book Le Corset: étude physiologique et pratique.[1][2]

The defining change was a long straight-fronted busk that supported and raised the abdomen instead of compressing it, removing the inward curve at the waist and leaving the chest free. The shape came mainly from the cut of the fabric rather than heavy boning.[2]

For people who care about how they look, the garment shaped the fashionable silhouette of about 1900 to 1908, which was a flat front, forward-pushed bust and hips set back, often called the S-bend. Fashion historians say that name is a later label, and that the exaggerated S-curve was a fashion development of her design rather than her intention.[2][3]

chain: Long straight busk supports the abdomen
Torso is pushed upright and tilted forward
angle.text: While worn, the corset shapes the torso and posture into the fashionable c. 1900 profile. The effect lasts only while it is worn.

paras: According to the Fashion Institute of Technology's fashion history account, Gaches-Sarraute began developing a supportive corset from 1890 for patients with gynaecological problems, and by 1896 had given a conference and distributed pamphlets to journalists. Her goal was to relieve pressure on the diaphragm and abdomen, including the reproductive organs.[2]

The straight-fronted busk supported and raised the abdomen. Shape came mostly from the cut of the fabric, including bias-cut gores, with flexible boning mainly keeping it smooth, and many health corsets of the period fastened with buttons instead of metal busks.[2]

The silhouette developed gradually: backs began arching by 1896, skirt fronts flattened by 1897, and the fashionable shape was established by 1899, peaking around 1900 and lasting more than a decade.[2] Wikipedia dates the style to about 1900 to 1908, and a 1902 diagram of a straight-front corset is reproduced there.[3] The term S-bend is described as anachronistic and traced to a short-lived 1905 posing fad.[2]

The look depended on stance as well as the garment. Dr. Lydia Ross promoted "poise" to help women achieve the correct posture.[2] From 1908 to 1914 a narrow-hipped fashion led to longer corsets that reached the thighs, anticipating the 1920s silhouette, and rubberized elastic developed in 1911 helped the girdle replace the corset.[3]

Gaches-Sarraute intended the corset as a medical device rather than a fashion item, and believed it would benefit women generally.[2] Later assessments differ: physician Robert Latou Dickinson reported in 1910 that S-line corsets still limited breathing from the diaphragm and pushed downward on the pelvis, and the FIT account concludes that the corset was not ultimately healthier than older styles.[2][3]

In 1901 Gaches-Sarraute lost a civil suit against the Maison Henri Vion, and the account notes that she may have collaborated with others or that other French doctors may have developed similar designs independently.[2]

No studies found. A treadmill test with historical reenactors reported significantly higher breathing and heart rates after exercise when wearing a 1900s-style straight-front corset, and a 1910 study by Robert Latou Dickinson described effects on breathing and the pelvis.[3]

timeline.event: Inès Gaches-Sarraute begins developing a supportive abdominal corset.[2]
She gives a conference and distributes pamphlets to journalists; backs begin arching in fashion.[2]
The straight-front silhouette is established in fashion.[2]
